text:
elaine.ops: heads-up — AcmeCorp reporting intermittent mTLS handshake failures to their Redwood Private control plane since yesterday after a corp firewall/NGFW update. Agents on their k8s nodes show TLS handshake errors and occasional 503s. They say other external services are fine.

matt.support: can you paste the agent log snippet and ask them to run a tcpdump + openssl s_client and attach? also which control plane hostname/IP are they hitting?

elaine.ops: log from one failing agent:``` 
2026-03-01T22:11:03Z agent: dial controlplane.redwood.local:443: handshake error: tls: remote error: handshake failure
agent: last_cert_chain: []
agent: got alert: unknown_ca
``` 
They hit controlplane.redwood.local -> 10.4.12.7 (VPC egress IP). They confirmed corp NGFW pushed a policy last night.

raj.engineer: "unknown_ca" is interesting — that suggests the server rejected the client cert, not server cert validation. Two common causes: 1) the NGFW is terminating TLS and re-originating upstream (so client cert never reaches control plane), or 2) the proxy is mangling/reordering the client cert chain so the control plane can't map to a trusted CA. Any chance the proxy is inserting its own intermediate?

elaine.ops: customer says the NGFW is doing TLS inspection and they rotated an intermediate CA recently (corp-intermediate). They also mentioned a transparent proxy that adds corp-intermediate.pem.

matt.support: ask them to run this from a failing node and paste output:```bash
openssl s_client -connect controlplane.redwood.local:443 -servername controlplane.redwood.local -showcerts -alpn h2
```
We need to see verify errors and the certificate chain the client sees.

elaine.ops: they ran it and returned:```
CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=0 CN = redwood-controlplane
verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
verify return:1
---
Certificate chain
 0 s:/CN=redwood-controlplane
   i:/CN=corp-intermediate
 1 s:/CN=corp-intermediate
   i:/CN=corp-root
---
SSL handshake has read 1024 bytes and written 512 bytes
verify return:1
```
They also captured a tcpdump. Annotated excerpt from their capture:```
[client -> proxy] ClientHello (requests Certificate)
[proxy -> controlplane] ClientHello (no certificate request extension seen by capture)
[client -> proxy] Certificate (client sent cert)
[proxy -> controlplane] no client Certificate forwarded (proxy terminated TLS)
```

raj.engineer: that pattern is a classic TLS-inspect re-encrypt scenario: proxy terminates client TLS, then opens a new TLS session to control plane without forwarding the client cert. For mTLS to work, the proxy must be configured for passthrough or to forward the original client cert (e.g., via header) and the control plane must accept that header (rare).

matt.support: quick checks for customer to run: 1) from a test host that bypasses NGFW, confirm mTLS works (same client cert/key). 2) on NGFW, look for "SSL Forward Proxy" vs "SSL Passthrough" mode — passthrough is required for true mutual TLS. 3) get proxy logs for entries like `SSL handshake terminated` or `client certificate not provided`.

elaine.ops: they tried bypassing the NGFW from a jump host and mTLS succeeds. On the NGFW they found a decryption profile that terminates and re-encrypts. NGFW logs show: `ssl-decrypt: handshake-terminated, client-certificate-not-forwarded`.

raj.engineer: options to resolve:
- Preferred: configure NGFW for TLS passthrough for traffic to controlplane.redwood.local (SNI or IP-based) so client side certs reach our control plane unchanged.
- If passthrough not possible: update corporate policy to preserve client certificate and forward it to upstream (if their NGFW supports Certificate Forwarding).
- Temporary workaround: add the NGFW's re-originating intermediate (corp-intermediate) to the control plane truststore so the control plane will accept the proxied chain — only safe if org policy allows and you trust the NGFW to assert identity.

matt.support: sample Palo Alto policy guidance (customer uses PA): add an exception to Decryption Policy with Source/Destination/SVC matching controlplane.redwood.local and set Decryption to `No Decrypt` for that rule. Or add the control plane host to the Decryption Exclusion list.

elaine.ops: customer asked for exact steps for AWS Private deployment: they can add an egress security rule to allow direct outbound to 10.4.12.7:443 from control-plane subnets and restrict NGFW inspection for that CIDR. We'll send sample iptables/sg lines.

raj.engineer: if they cannot reconfigure their NGFW, escalate to enterprise-svc: we can accept the proxy's intermediate cert in truststore after legal/infosec review. Also we can provide a short-lived alternate endpoint for them to test passthrough without changing prod policies.

matt.support: next action: @elaine.ops please ask them to try No Decrypt for controlplane.redwood.local and report tcpdump & agent logs. If they confirm passthrough fixes it, we'll document a recommended Decryption Exclusion with step-by-step for PA and F5. :thumbsup:

sre-bot: ticket #INC-2026-214 created for tracking, assigned to raj.engineer, priority P2.

elaine.ops: customer will test bypass tonight and update. I'll post results here. Thanks team! :pray:
